title: Single-Molecule Imaging of Transcription and Epigenetic Factors in Human Neural Stem Cells
author: Atsumi, Yamamoto, et al.

steps.title: Import time‑series image into ImageJ
steps.instruction: Open the SIF file (generated by Solis software) containing a 256 × 256‑pixel image series via ImageJ → Plugins → Andor → Read SIF.

steps.title: Select image frames for analysis
steps.instruction: Choose the number of consecutive frames to analyse; if left unchanged the default is 1200 frames corresponding to 2 min of observation.

steps.title: Subtract image background (optional)
steps.instruction: Run ImageJ → Process → Subtract Background and set an appropriate pixel value to reduce background; skip this step if the raw images already have low background.

steps.title: Detect single‑molecule spots with PTA
steps.instruction: Launch the Particle Tracking Analysis plugin (Plugins → PTA → PTA Particle Track and Analysis, version 1) and set the following parameters:

substeps.instruction: ROI size (x, y) of searching area: 9 × 9 pixels
Pixel size of minimal spots: 3 pixels

steps.title: Verify PTA spot detection
steps.instruction: Visually inspect the rectangles drawn by PTA over the image series (see Methods video S1) to confirm that detected CREB spots correspond to real fluorescence signals.

steps.title: Export spot parameters to Excel
steps.instruction: Save the PTA result table, which includes centre coordinates and dwell times for each spot, and import the data into an Excel worksheet.

steps.title: Fit residence‑time distribution in Origin
steps.instruction: Open Origin 9.1, plot the cumulative residence‑time distribution from the Excel data, and fit it with the biexponential function F(t)=A0+A1{1−exp(−t/t1)}+A2{1−exp(−t/t2)}. Ensure the chi‑square tolerance of the fit is < 1 × 10⁻⁹.

steps.title: Import CREB and CBP image files for colocalization
steps.instruction: Load the TMR‑CREB (HaloTag) and SNAP‑CBP ND2 files into ImageJ as separate image stacks.

steps.title: Detect CREB spots (repeat PTA settings)
steps.instruction: Apply the PTA plugin to the CREB image stack using the same parameters listed in step 4.

steps.title: Filter long‑residence CREB spots
steps.instruction: In the PTA result table, sort the spots by dwell time (frame length) and select those with dwell time > 1 s (long‑residence spots).

steps.title: Obtain CREB localisation statistics
steps.instruction: Highlight each long‑residence CREB row, choose Statistics → Show Statistics, and record averageX, sdX, averageY, sdY (also point index, total frame, run length, averageFI, sdFI).

steps.title: Calculate CREB localisation error circles
steps.instruction: For each long‑residence CREB spot, compute the localisation‑error radius as the larger of 1.96 × sdX or 1.96 × sdY; the centre of the circle is (averageX, averageY).

steps.title: Detect and process CBP spots
steps.instruction: Run PTA on the CBP image stack (same parameters), extract XY coordinates and localisation errors for long‑residence CBP spots using the same procedure as for CREB.

steps.title: Determine CREB‑CBP colocalization
steps.instruction: For each time point where a long‑residence CREB and a long‑residence CBP spot are present, declare them colocalized if the CREB error circle overlaps the CBP error circle (i.e., distance between centres < sum of their localisation‑error radii).

description: Protein-DNA and protein-protein interactions are important issues in understanding transcription mechanisms.2,3,4 Highly inclined and laminated optical sheet (HILO) microscopy in combination with HaloTag and/or SNAP-tag proteins and their fluorescent ligands is an excellent experimental approach to observe the spatiotemporal dynamics of proteins, such as transcription and epigenetic factors in the nucleus, in living cells at the single-molecule level (Figure 1).5,6,7,8,9,10,11 Here we demonstrate a detailed method of single-molecule imaging (SMI) to reveal the behavior of the transcription factor cAMP response element binding protein (CREB) and the histone acetyltransferase CREB binding protein (CBP)12,13,14,15,16 in human neural stem cell (NSC)-derived neurons.17,18,19 This protocol can be used for a variety of primary cells and cell lines and can be applied to the studies of diverse intracellular proteins including nuclear proteins.Figure 1Schematic of HILO microscopyAn incident laser beam, controlled by a movable mirror, is positioned to propagate near the edge of the 100× oil-immersion objective lens, and the resulting HILO illuminates nuclei in a single cell cultured on a glass-bottom dish. Fluorescent signals with low background noise from the fluorescence-tagged proteins through the same objective lens are captured by an EMCCD camera.
